FrMS88-de5322-d1e111.summary: Poses the fifteenth question: whether abstractive knowledge of the divine essence, not of its existence, can be communicated to a wayfarer. Against: Dionysius says divine realities are not knowable. For: (Dionysius ch. 1) the good is communicable.
claims: Dionysius seems to deny that divine realities are knowable.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e131.summary: Announces two inquiries: what abstractive knowledge is, and whether it can be communicated. Reports a definition: abstractive knowledge is of a thing in some representative when the thing cannot be had present.
claims: Reported definition: abstractive cognition is of the thing as in a representative.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e144.summary: Argues against that definition: the object as in a representative is not distinct from the representative (Augustine), and knowledge does not terminate at a likeness; the object is said to be in the species only because the species stands in for it as moving cause, not as terminus; if the species is terminus, nothing would be known but what is in the intellect; and the object there has only intentional being, so it would be known only as in the species or the species alone would be known.
claims: Abstractive knowledge cannot terminate at the object merely as it is in the species.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e173.summary: Gives his own account: abstractive knowledge is of a thing through a representative, but terminates at the quiddity of the object in itself and what belongs to it per se — and per se nothing belongs to a thing as outside or inside the soul, but as it is in itself abstracted.
claims: Abstractive cognition terminates at the quiddity in itself, abstracted from existence in or outside the soul.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e185.summary: Raises four objections: species are known abstractively, which would require infinite representatives; intuitive eye-vision also occurs through a species, so this cannot define abstractive cognition; one seeing oneself in a mirror sees either abstractively (absurdly by an external sense) or intuitively through a species; God sees future contingents intuitively in a representative, and the blessed see creatures in the Word.
claims: Objection: representation through a species does not distinguish abstractive from intuitive cognition.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e216.summary: Reply to the first: a species is known properly only argumentatively, not through a representative; starting from intuitive experience that I understand, which requires something present in the soul that is not the thing, I infer that the species is in me.
claims: Species are known only by inference from the experience of understanding.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e229.summary: Reply to the second: in sight, the species and the vision are two essentially ordered effects of the same cause (like illuminating and heating), both caused by the object; the vision is not caused by the species.
claims: In vision, species and seeing are both effects of the object.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e240.summary: Reply to the third: one seeing oneself in a mirror intuits oneself immediately by a reflected act, though the external sense judges there is a species there, being used to seeing in a straight line.
claims: Mirror vision is immediate intuition by reflection.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e251.summary: Reply to the fourth reports views: some say God knows abstractively what he knows through his essence but knows his essence intuitively, which Meyronnes rejects since abstractive knowledge implies imperfection; others that knowledge is named from its first object, so God's act is wholly intuitive; 'another doctor of ours' that abstractive knowledge is in a determinate, not supereminent, representative, whereas the divine essence represents things eminently, more truly than they are in themselves, so contingents are known intuitively. Then turns to communicability, distinguishing four intellects (conjoined, separated in pure nature; elevated short of beatitude; wholly supernaturally elevated), and gives the first conclusion: our conjoined intellect cannot naturally have a proper and specific knowledge of deity.
claims: Abstractive knowledge implies imperfection and so is not in God.
The divine essence represents things eminently, so God knows contingents intuitively.
Our conjoined intellect cannot naturally know deity under its proper and specific notion.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e290.summary: Proves the first conclusion four ways: knowing a quiddity's proper notion includes knowing its aptitudes, so we would know the essence is communicable to three; it includes knowing its natural active power, so we would know naturally that creation (and incarnation) is possible; we do not even know many created quiddities by proper differences, only extraneous ones; and we would know naturally what is really identical with the divine quiddity, the personal properties. Second conclusion: our intellect elevated supernaturally short of beatitude can know the divine essence under its proper and specific notion through an infused species.
claims: Natural knowledge of deity's proper notion would entail natural knowledge of the Trinity and the possibility of creation.
We know many created quiddities only through extraneous differences.
An intellect elevated short of beatitude can know the divine essence properly by an infused species.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e337.summary: First proof of the second conclusion: memory, intellect, and will are adequate powers, so what one can the other can; Paul's memory had an act of recollection of his vision, through a species, so the intellect too could know distinctly by such a species. Reports a reply that Paul saw distinctly but remembered indistinctly, as shown by 'whether in the body or out of the body I do not know'.
claims: Paul's recollection of his rapture shows a species of the divine essence was in his memory.
Reported reply: Paul remembered only indistinctly.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e357.summary: Argues against the reply: an indistinct concept is of the definitum and a distinct concept of the definition; whoever has the concept of the subject of a self-evident proposition can have the concept of its predicate, and definitum and definition form a self-evident proposition; so one with an indistinct concept of the divine essence can acquire a distinct one, and Paul had an indistinct one.
claims: Whoever has an indistinct concept of something can acquire a distinct one.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e381.summary: Argues similarly for obscure and clear knowledge, since Paul knew the essence and nothing else. Second proof: what God can do through a secondary cause he can do himself (noted as a weak argument inserted by others). Third: if a greater perfection is not repugnant to a creature neither is a lesser; attaining an object by an act is more perfect than by a species. Fourth: divine entity and deity are equally infinite, and divine entity can be represented by a species, so deity can. Third conclusion: a separated intellect in pure nature can reach proper knowledge of the divine essence — since it can know every limited being, including a species God might cause representing the divine essence; it can know complex acts having the divine essence as subject; it can know the beatific habit whose subject is the divine essence; and it can know all relations of creatures to God and thus their term.
claims: What a creature can attain by a more perfect act it can attain by a less perfect representation.
Divine entity and deity are equally infinite, so if one can be represented by a species, so can the other.
A separated intellect in pure nature can attain proper knowledge of the divine essence.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e470.summary: Considers a reply: God is known only as terminating such relations, under a general notion or one other than deity.
claims: Reported reply: creatures' relations to God terminate at him under a general notion.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e479.summary: Rejects it: whoever understands a relation understands its term as its term, and the creature's relation to God as ultimate end and beatifier terminates at God under the proper notion of deity. The only possible response would be to deny the supposition, which he therefore proves: a separated intellect intuiting creatures knows what is accidental to them (like place), so a fortiori their per se relations to God. Fourth conclusion: a separated and elevated intellect can see and know God, supported by Augustine (angels' morning knowledge in the Word), Origen on Isaiah (Isaiah saw God neither intuitively nor merely by faith), the revelation to John of propositions with God as subject, and Gregory on Adam's recollection of what he saw in sleep. Then raises Dionysius' objection that lower-order species cannot represent higher-order realities.
claims: The creature's relation to God as ultimate end terminates at God under the proper notion of deity.
A separated intellect that knows creatures intuitively can know their per se relations to God.
A separated, elevated intellect can see and know God.
Objection: lower species cannot represent higher realities.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e549.summary: Reply: to represent is not to have formally in oneself but only to move to an act in which there is perfect likeness in representing, not in being; moving to an act concerning the divine essence is a limited cognition and can be done imperfectly.
claims: Representation requires only moving the intellect to an act, not formal possession of what is represented.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e561.summary: Answers the objection that as thing exceeds thing so likeness exceeds likeness, and the infinite infinitely exceeds the finite: everyone must solve this, since all hold that the beatific act is a perfect likeness of the divine essence; no adequation is required, only a proportion, as an accidental representative may represent a substance.
claims: Representation requires proportion, not adequation.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e579.summary: Second objection: things equally infinite are equally knowable naturally or not; divine entity is as infinite as deity, and deity cannot be known naturally.
claims: Objection: divine entity and deity, equally infinite, must be equally unknowable.

FrMS88-de5322-d1e588.summary: Reply: this takes as cause what is not the cause; deity cannot be naturally known not because of its infinity, but because even the specific notions or differences of created things are unknown to us, so much more this one.
claims: Our natural ignorance of deity is due not to its infinity but to our ignorance of specific differences.

FrMS88-de5322.summary: The fifteenth question of the prologue asks whether abstractive knowledge of the divine essence, not bearing on its existence, can be communicated to a wayfarer. Meyronnes first defines abstractive cognition: rejecting the account that it knows the thing 'as in a representative' (since the object as in the species is not distinct from the species, and knowledge would then terminate at the species or at merely intentional being), he holds that it is knowledge of a thing through a representative but terminates at the quiddity of the object in itself, abstracted from existence inside and outside the soul. He defends this against objections (species are known only argumentatively from the experience of understanding; in vision species and seeing are co-effects of the object; the mirror case is reflexive intuition; God's knowledge of contingents is intuitive because the divine essence represents eminently). On communicability he distinguishes four intellects — conjoined and separated in pure nature, elevated short of beatitude, and wholly elevated — and argues four conclusions: (1) our conjoined intellect cannot naturally have a proper, specific concept of deity, else it would know the communicability of the essence to three persons, the possibility of creation, and the persons themselves; (2) our intellect supernaturally elevated short of beatitude can, by an infused species, know the divine essence under its proper notion, as in Paul's rapture, whose memory and possible distinct concept show this; (3) a separated intellect in pure nature can attain proper knowledge of the divine essence, since it can know every limited thing, including species representing deity and the creature's relations to God as ultimate end, which terminate at God under the proper notion of deity; (4) an elevated separated intellect can see and know God, supported by Augustine's morning knowledge, Origen on Isaiah, John's revelation, and Gregory on Adam. He answers Dionysius' objection that lower species cannot represent higher realities by holding that representation requires only moving the intellect to an act, not equality, and attributes our natural ignorance of deity not to its infinity but to our ignorance of even the specific differences of creatures.
claims: Abstractive cognition is knowledge through a representative that terminates at the object's quiddity in itself, abstracting from existence.
Species are known only argumentatively, not through another representative.
Our intellect in this life cannot naturally attain a proper and specific concept of deity.
An intellect supernaturally elevated short of beatitude can know the divine essence under its proper notion through an infused species.
A separated intellect in pure nature can attain proper knowledge of the divine essence.
Representation does not require equality between the representation and what is represented.
Our natural ignorance of deity stems from our ignorance of specific differences, not from divine infinity.
